events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: Bhola Cyclone
events.blurb: A tropical cyclone with 185 km/h winds made landfall on the low-lying islands of the Bay of Bengal delta at high tide, driving a 10-metre storm surge over villages built at sea level. At least 300,000 people died, possibly up to 500,000 — the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history. The East Pakistan government's slow response fueled the separatist movement that led to war within months.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1970 — East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). The relief failure helped trigger the Bangladesh Liberation War the following March. The former Beatle George Harrison organized the Concert for Bangladesh to raise funds.

events.title: Bhopal Disaster
events.blurb: A cloud of methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a pesticide plant on the outskirts of a central Indian city shortly after midnight, drifting over densely populated slums whose inhabitants woke choking and blind. Between 8,000 and 16,000 people died in the immediate aftermath; 500,000 were injured. Groundwater at the site remains contaminated four decades on.
events.revealBlurb: December 2-3, 1984 — Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. The plant was owned by Union Carbide; the American parent company settled for $470 million, a fraction of the actual cost. The CEO, Warren Anderson, was briefly arrested and then quietly released; India's extradition requests were ignored.

events.title: Haiti Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck an impoverished Caribbean nation 25 kilometres from its capital, collapsing the presidential palace, the cathedral, and roughly 250,000 homes built to no meaningful engineering standards. Estimates of the dead range from 100,000 to 316,000 — about 3 percent of the country's population. The recovery was plagued by mismanagement and a cholera outbreak accidentally introduced by UN peacekeepers.
events.revealBlurb: January 12, 2010 — Port-au-Prince. International pledges totaled $13 billion; only a fraction was ever delivered or effectively spent. An estimated 1.5 million people were displaced. Nepalese UN troops inadvertently introduced cholera that killed another 10,000+ people over the following years.

events.title: Elizabeth Blackwell Graduates
events.blurb: A 28-year-old English-born schoolteacher, who had been admitted to a small upstate New York medical college as a joke when the all-male student body voted unanimously to accept her application, graduated first in her class to become the first woman in the United States to earn a medical degree. She had been refused admission by 20 other schools. Her younger sister would become the third.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1849 — Geneva Medical College, Geneva, NY. No American hospital would employ her; she moved to Paris and London for clinical training. She later founded a medical college for women and practiced for decades, treating patients the profession otherwise ignored.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Solos the Atlantic
events.blurb: A 34-year-old American aviator landed her red single-engine Lockheed Vega in a farmer's meadow in northern Ireland after a 15-hour, 3,260-kilometre flight from Newfoundland, becoming the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. The trip had included an altimeter failure, engine icing, and a broken exhaust manifold that spewed flames into the cockpit for the last eight hours.
events.revealBlurb: May 20-21, 1932 — exactly five years after Charles Lindbergh's crossing. Earhart had originally meant to land in Paris; she turned toward the nearest pasture when she smelled fuel. She had been the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air four years earlier, but only as a passenger.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Disappears
events.blurb: On the penultimate leg of an around-the-world flight at the equator, a 39-year-old American aviator and her navigator took off from a Pacific airstrip bound for a tiny coral island 4,100 kilometres away. Her final radio messages reported low fuel and inability to locate the island. A Navy search of 400,000 square kilometres of ocean found nothing. Her disappearance has launched a hundred books and at least three feature films.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1937 — Earhart and Fred Noonan bound for Howland Island. Prevailing theories: ran out of fuel and ditched; landed on uninhabited Nikumaroro and died of thirst; captured by the Japanese. No conclusive physical evidence exists.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Benazir Bhutto Becomes PM
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Oxford and Harvard educated politician whose father had been hanged by a previous military government was sworn in as prime minister of a large South Asian Muslim-majority country, becoming the first woman to head the government of any Muslim-majority state. Her ruling coalition was fragile; she would be dismissed twice on corruption charges and would be assassinated 19 years later while campaigning for a third term.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1988 — Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan. She was assassinated in Rawalpindi on December 27, 2007, after a campaign rally. Her 19-year-old son Bilawal was named co-chair of her party within days.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: First Woman in Space
events.blurb: Valentina Tereshkova, a 26-year-old former textile factory worker and amateur parachutist with no pilot training, launched aboard Vostok 6 and orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days — more total time in space than all US astronauts who had flown to that date combined. She performed observations and photographed aerosol layers in Earth's atmosphere before parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Tereshkova selected herself from 400 applicants by writing a letter directly to the Soviet Space Program. She reportedly got motion sick and did not conduct some planned manual maneuvers, a fact kept classified for years. No woman flew in space again for 19 years. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

events.title: Galileo Enters Jupiter Orbit
events.blurb: NASA's Galileo spacecraft became the first to orbit an outer planet when it fired its main engine for 49 minutes to slow into Jupiter orbit. Simultaneously, a 339 kg atmospheric probe it had released five months earlier plunged into Jupiter's clouds and transmitted data for 58 minutes, surviving temperatures of 16,000 °C before being crushed by atmospheric pressure.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1995 — Galileo. The spacecraft's high-gain antenna failed to deploy fully in 1991, so the entire mission's data was re-routed through a low-gain antenna; engineers compressed the transmission protocols so thoroughly that Galileo sent back almost as much science as originally planned. During its eight years at Jupiter, it discovered evidence of a liquid water ocean beneath Europa's ice.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: First Orbital Rocket Booster Landing
events.blurb: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage returned from an orbital-class mission and landed upright at Landing Zone 1 in Cape Canaveral, completing the first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster under propulsive control. The same vehicle had delivered 11 commercial satellites to orbit minutes earlier and touched down within about 10 meters of the target pad.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2015 — OG-2 Mission 2. SpaceX had attempted and failed four previous booster landings on a drone ship at sea. The Falcon's legs deployed at 180 m altitude. Elon Musk posted one word after confirmation: "Welcome back, baby." The reused booster concept cut launch costs by roughly 30%.

events.title: First Soviet Atomic Bomb Test
events.blurb: Four years after U.S. weapons ended the Pacific war, Soviet scientists detonated their own plutonium implosion device at a test range in the Kazakh steppe. Western intelligence had predicted the breakthrough was at least five years away. The explosion ended the American nuclear monopoly and opened the arms race.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1949 — codename RDS-1, nicknamed "First Lightning." The design was largely cribbed from the U.S. Fat Man bomb via spy networks inside the Manhattan Project. Klaus Fuchs had handed over detailed blueprints.

events.title: Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan
events.blurb: Thousands of Soviet paratroopers and mechanized divisions crossed into a central Asian country to prop up a failing Marxist government, assassinating the sitting president in the process and installing a more pliable replacement. The operation was supposed to last weeks. Instead it dragged on for nearly a decade, bleeding the Soviet treasury, radicalizing a generation of fighters, and helping bring the superpower down.
events.revealBlurb: December 24-27, 1979 — the intervention cost the USSR an estimated 15,000 dead and 35,000 wounded. The US, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan funneled billions in arms to the mujahideen, some of whom would later form al-Qaeda.

events.title: KAL 007 Shot Down
events.blurb: A Korean civilian airliner carrying 269 passengers and crew strayed over Soviet airspace over the Sea of Japan on a flight from New York to Seoul. A Sukhoi interceptor fired two air-to-air missiles and the 747 broke apart over international waters. The Kremlin at first denied any involvement; the United States released taped radio transmissions of the shootdown within a week.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1983 — a U.S. congressman, Larry McDonald, was among the dead. Reagan called it an "act of barbarism." The incident led directly to the U.S. decision to make GPS available for civilian use, so no passenger aircraft would ever again stray for lack of navigation.

events.title: Chernobyl Disaster
events.blurb: During a safety test at the No. 4 reactor of a Ukrainian nuclear power plant, a power surge, flawed reactor design, and operator errors combined to blow the 1,000-tonne reactor lid off the building and send a radioactive plume across Europe. Swedish sensors detected the contamination before Moscow admitted anything had happened. The exclusion zone around the plant remains largely uninhabited nearly forty years on.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1986 — 1:23 AM. Two workers died in the initial explosion; 28 firefighters and operators died of acute radiation poisoning in the months after. Roughly 350,000 people were permanently evacuated. Cleanup cost the USSR an estimated 18 billion rubles.

events.title: INF Treaty Signed
events.blurb: At a White House ceremony, the American and Soviet leaders signed a treaty requiring both sides to destroy every intermediate-range nuclear missile they possessed — the first arms-control agreement that actually cut existing weapons rather than capping their growth. Within three years, 2,692 missiles had been verifiably dismantled.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1987 — Reagan and Gorbachev. Both Pershing IIs and SS-20s were eliminated. The treaty was abandoned in 2019 after mutual accusations of cheating, ending a 32-year cornerstone of European security.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Mozart's Requiem Unfinished
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Austrian composer who had been commissioned by a mysterious stranger six months earlier to compose a requiem Mass for an anonymous client died in his Vienna apartment with the work unfinished. Much of the "Dies irae" and "Lacrimosa" had been sketched only. His widow, in desperate financial circumstances, had a student complete the work to secure the remaining half of the commission fee.
events.revealBlurb: December 5, 1791 — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, aged 35. The mysterious stranger was Count Walsegg, who meant to pass the work off as his own for his late wife. Mozart's student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it; his contributions have been debated ever since.

events.title: Altamont Free Concert
events.blurb: A free Rolling Stones concert at a dusty California motor speedway, hastily organized as a West Coast Woodstock, instead became the counterculture's dark counterpart. Hells Angels motorcycle gang members had been hired to provide stage security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. Fights broke out throughout the day; during the Rolling Stones' set an Angel stabbed an 18-year-old audience member to death within a metre of the stage.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1969 — Altamont Speedway, California. The victim was Meredith Hunter, 18; the Angel who stabbed him, Alan Passaro, was acquitted on grounds of self-defense. The 1970 documentary "Gimme Shelter" captures the killing.

events.title: Rapper's Delight Released
events.blurb: Three rappers from the New York metro area, assembled by an independent label, released a 15-minute track over a bassline lifted from a recent disco hit. It was the first hip-hop single to reach the U.S. Billboard Top 40. The culture it came from had been thriving in parks and clubs around the Bronx for six years; this record introduced it to mainstream white America and set rap on the path from subcultural movement to dominant global genre.
events.revealBlurb: September 1979 — Sugarhill Gang on Sugar Hill Records. The bassline was from Chic's "Good Times"; Chic's Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards sued and received co-writing credit. The track went platinum in the US and hit #3 in the UK.

events.title: John Lennon Shot
events.blurb: A 40-year-old former Beatle, returning to his Manhattan apartment building with his wife after a late-night recording session, was shot four times in the back at close range by a young man he had signed an autograph for earlier that afternoon. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital 20 minutes later. Vigils were held around the world. His wife asked that his birthday be celebrated with international moments of silence, which has since become a yearly tradition.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1980 — John Lennon at The Dakota, NYC. Shooter Mark David Chapman remains in prison, denied parole 13 times. Lennon's album "Double Fantasy" had been released three weeks earlier; it took on enormous posthumous sales.

events.title: The Mother of All Demos
events.blurb: A 43-year-old Stanford Research Institute engineer delivered a 90-minute live demonstration to 1,000 conference attendees in San Francisco that showcased a computing system combining the mouse, windowing interface, hypertext links, real-time text editing, screen sharing, and video conferencing — all two decades before any of these became available on a commercial computer. The audience sat in stunned silence.
events.revealBlurb: December 9, 1968 — Douglas Engelbart at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. His live video link from his Menlo Park lab used four microwave stations. Xerox PARC, founded in 1970, hired many of his team; Apple later hired Xerox's. Engelbart's lab invented it all first.

events.title: First Cellular Phone Call
events.blurb: A Motorola engineer, standing on a Manhattan street with a 1.1-kilogram "brick" prototype handset to his ear, placed a phone call to his chief rival at a competing company's research lab — and made sure to inform him what he was doing. The handset's battery gave 35 minutes of talk time after 10 hours of charging. Motorola would spend another decade getting a lighter version to market.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1973 — Martin Cooper of Motorola called Joel Engel at Bell Labs. The prototype was the DynaTAC 8000x. It sold commercially in 1983 for $3,995. Cooper later said he'd been inspired by the communicator in Star Trek.

events.title: IBM Personal Computer Launched
events.blurb: A technology corporation released a personal computer based on an Intel processor running an operating system licensed from a small software company for $25,000. Its open architecture allowed third-party manufacturers to build compatible clones, spawning a global personal computer industry worth trillions within a decade.

events.title: Deep Blue Beats Kasparov
events.blurb: An IBM chess-playing computer, running on a 480-processor supercomputer in New York and evaluating 200 million positions per second, defeated the reigning world chess champion in the sixth game of a six-game match. The loss — the first time a computer had defeated a world champion in a regulation match — the champion afterward accused IBM of cheating by having grandmasters intervene in the machine's moves, which IBM denied. IBM retired the machine immediately after the match.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1997 — Deep Blue vs. Garry Kasparov, New York. Final match score: 3.5–2.5 Deep Blue. The specific "intuition" move that shocked Kasparov (game 2, move 37) was later attributed to a bug in the code forcing a fallback routine.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: Monroe Doctrine Declared
events.blurb: An American president's annual address to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or political interference in the Western Hemisphere, a policy the United States could not yet militarily enforce but would cite for the next two centuries. The message was drafted largely by his Secretary of State, a future president himself.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1823 — James Monroe. The phrase "Monroe Doctrine" wasn't coined until 1850. Britain quietly backed the policy because it suited their own trade interests, and for decades the Royal Navy did most of the actual enforcing.

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Machiavelli Writes The Prince
events.blurb: An unemployed former Florentine civil servant, exiled from the city after a change of regime, wrote a compact political treatise in the form of advice to a hereditary ruler on how to acquire and maintain power. Its flat, unsentimental analysis of the uses of cruelty, deception, and popular love versus fear shocked readers and made its author's name a by-word for cynical politics. It remained unpublished until five years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: 1513 — Niccolò Machiavelli. The treatise was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, who almost certainly never read it. Published 1532 and promptly placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Still in print 500 years later.

events.title: Pride and Prejudice Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old unmarried English rector's daughter living quietly with her widowed mother in Hampshire published, anonymously, her second novel — a comedy of manners about five daughters of a small landowner, an arrogant wealthy suitor, and a perceptive heroine who misreads them both. The first edition of 1,500 copies was a modest success; the author made £140 from it. She would die four years later; her anonymity was preserved until a posthumous edition named her.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1813 — Jane Austen, attributed to "By the Author of Sense and Sensibility." She sold the copyright outright for £110; her estate never profited further. Austen is now the most continuously read English novelist. A first edition sold at auction in 2008 for £105,000.

events.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
events.blurb: A Swedish Academy of cultural grandees, following the will of the dynamite inventor who had died five years earlier leaving his fortune to fund annual prizes, selected a 62-year-old French poet as the first recipient of their literature award. Their choice was safe, genteel, and now obscure; they had passed over Leo Tolstoy, widely considered Europe's greatest living novelist. The omission has dogged the Nobel Literature Prize's reputation ever since.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1901 — Sully Prudhomme. Other early laureates passed over: Tolstoy, Chekhov, Ibsen, Zola, Mark Twain. The prize included 150,782 Swedish kronor — a substantial sum in 1901, about $3.5 million today.

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: MTV First Broadcast
events.blurb: A music video channel began broadcasting at 12:01 a.m., opening with a brief spoken introduction before playing a three-minute clip of a rock band performing against footage of a rocket launch. The first words spoken on air were "Ladies and gentlemen, rock and roll" — the channel ran continuously for 24 hours with no advertisements.

events.title: Thriller Album Released
events.blurb: A recording artist released a 42-minute album featuring nine tracks, seven of which became top-ten singles on the Billboard Hot 100 — a chart achievement never matched before or since. The album sold more than 66 million copies, and its 14-minute title-track music video transformed the medium from a promotional clip into an art form.

events.title: Cabbage Patch Kids Craze
events.blurb: Mass-marketed soft dolls with distinctive rotund faces, each shipped with an individual "birth certificate" and name, became the must-have Christmas gift of the holiday shopping season in the United States. Retail stampedes, fights, and injuries were reported as parents competed to buy the limited supplies of the dolls — Coleco had grossly underestimated demand. Adjusted for population, Cabbage Patch Kids may have sold more units in their peak years than any toy ever.
events.revealBlurb: December 1983 — Coleco. Xavier Roberts had been selling hand-sewn versions ("Little People") at craft fairs for years before the mass-market deal. Riots and fights occurred at multiple US stores; Coleco sold about 3 million dolls in 1983 and 20 million by the end of 1984.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: Marie Curie Wins Nobel Prize
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Polish-born physicist working in a converted shed in a French capital became the first woman to win the world's most prestigious scientific prize, sharing a physics award with her husband and a French colleague for their research into radioactivity. She would win it a second time, alone, in chemistry eight years later. Her notebooks are still radioactive, stored in lead-lined boxes and read only in protective clothing.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1903 — shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She later became the first person, of any gender, to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her daughter Irène won a Nobel in chemistry too.

events.title: Jeannette Rankin Elected to Congress
events.blurb: A 36-year-old social worker and suffrage organizer from a western U.S. state was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives, becoming the first woman to hold federal office in the country. She took office four years before women nationally could vote. She would vote against entering both world wars — the only member of Congress to do so twice.
events.revealBlurb: November 7, 1916 — Montana had given women the state vote in 1914. Rankin's 1941 "no" vote on the declaration of war against Japan made her a pariah; she had to be escorted to her office by the Capitol police. "As a woman I can't go to war," she said, "and I refuse to send anyone else."

events.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.blurb: The United Nations General Assembly, meeting in a Paris exhibition hall, adopted a declaration of 30 articles enumerating rights that every human being was to be considered entitled to by virtue of humanity itself. The document's drafting committee, chaired by the widow of a U.S. president, had spent two years negotiating across ideological and cultural lines. No state voted against; eight abstained.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1948 — Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. Adopted 48-0 with 8 abstentions (Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia, South Africa). Translated into over 500 languages — more than any other document. December 10 is now International Human Rights Day.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Red Cross Founded
events.blurb: A committee of five Swiss citizens, led by a Geneva businessman who had witnessed the aftermath of a bloody Italian battle four years earlier and published a book about the unimaginable suffering of wounded soldiers left untreated on the field, established an international humanitarian organization to provide medical care to the wounded in war. Their emblem — a red cross on a white field, the Swiss flag inverted — was chosen as a neutral symbol protecting aid workers.
events.revealBlurb: February 17, 1863 — International Committee of the Red Cross, founded by Henry Dunant and four others in Geneva. Dunant won the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901 despite being nearly penniless. The Muslim world adopted the Red Crescent in 1876; Israel uses a Red Crystal, adopted 2005.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Insulin Administered to a Patient
events.blurb: A 14-year-old diabetic patient near death at a Toronto hospital received an injection of pancreatic extract prepared by two medical researchers after earlier formulations had failed due to impurities. The boy recovered, and researchers moved ward to ward injecting the remaining diabetic patients — transforming a death sentence into a manageable condition within weeks.

events.title: First Test-Tube Baby
events.blurb: A baby girl was delivered by caesarean section at a Lancashire hospital — the first human born via in vitro fertilization. Her conception had involved an egg retrieved from her mother, fertilized in a laboratory dish, and implanted in the uterus nine years after the research team had first proposed the technique. The birth prompted intense ethical debate and religious protest. By 2020, about 1 percent of the world's babies were born via IVF.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1978 — Louise Brown at Oldham General Hospital. Pioneers: Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe, Jean Purdy. Edwards won the Nobel Prize in 2010 at age 85; Steptoe and Purdy had died. Brown herself had a second son born naturally in 2013.

events.title: First COVID-19 Vaccine Authorized
events.blurb: The US Food and Drug Administration issued an emergency use authorization for a novel mRNA-based vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, developed in less than a year from the publication of the virus's genetic sequence — a timescale previously thought impossible for a vaccine. The mRNA technology, which instructs the body's own cells to produce viral spike protein that the immune system then learns to recognize, had been in development for decades but had never been used in a licensed vaccine.
events.revealBlurb: December 11, 2020 — Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Moderna's similar mRNA vaccine followed December 18. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, whose basic mRNA research had been neglected for years, won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Over 13 billion COVID vaccine doses were administered globally in the first three years.

events.title: Cotton Gin Patented
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Yale-educated New Englander, tutoring at a Georgia plantation, built a simple wooden cylinder with wire teeth that combed cotton seeds out of fibres 50 times faster than a slave's fingers could. He patented the device. Rather than being royally enriched, he spent years litigating piracy; the design was too simple to protect. The invention made short-staple cotton profitable across the American South, entrenching slavery economically just as it was weakening elsewhere.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1794 — Eli Whitney. He later pivoted to manufacturing muskets with interchangeable parts — an innovation that shaped the later assembly-line system. Demand for enslaved labour in the Deep South grew enormously between 1790 and 1860, in large part because of the gin.

events.title: Stockton & Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A steam locomotive hauling 21 coal wagons and one passenger coach completed a 40-kilometre journey through County Durham at a top speed of 24 km/h, carrying 450 passengers on its inaugural run. It was the first railway to carry both freight and fare-paying passengers using steam traction.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Marconi's Transatlantic Radio
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Italian-Irish electrical engineer and his assistants received, from a 300-metre wire antenna held aloft by a kite on a Newfoundland cliff, three short pulses — the letter S in Morse code — transmitted from a 25-kilowatt spark-gap generator in Cornwall, 3,400 kilometres away. The reception was brief, weak, and disputed by physicists who believed radio waves travelled only in straight lines and could not follow Earth's curvature. Subsequent experiments settled the argument.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 1901 — Guglielmo Marconi at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, receiving from Poldhu, Cornwall. He won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. The ionosphere's existence, which enables long-wave radio propagation around the planet, was not understood until the 1920s.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Completed
events.blurb: A German goldsmith completed printing a 1,286-page Latin Bible using a press with movable metal type, producing an estimated 180 copies at a rate no scribe could approach. Each sheet required individually set letter blocks cast in an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony — making it the first book in Europe produced by mechanical movable type.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: Council of Trent Opens
events.blurb: A general council of the Catholic Church, convened by the pope at a cathedral city in the Alpine foothills of northern Italy, opened with the task of responding to the Protestant Reformation. It met in three phases over 18 years, affirmed virtually every doctrine Protestants had rejected, standardized the Latin Mass, required bishops to reside in their dioceses, and launched the Counter-Reformation. Its decisions shaped Catholic practice for four centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 13, 1545 — opening of the Council of Trent. Its reforms hardened the Catholic/Protestant split rather than healing it. The Tridentine Latin Mass, established here, remained the standard form until the Second Vatican Council in 1965.

events.title: Spanish Armada Defeated
events.blurb: A Spanish naval force of 130 ships and 26,000 men, intended to escort a Flemish invasion army across the Channel to England, was met by a faster, more maneuverable English fleet off the Flanders coast. An English fireship attack scattered the Spanish anchorage overnight; the following day's running battle crippled the armada. Storms in the North Sea and along the Irish coast destroyed the rest on the long retreat home. Barely half returned to Spain.
events.revealBlurb: July 29 to August 8, 1588 — Battle of Gravelines decided it. English commanders: Lord Howard of Effingham, Sir Francis Drake. Roughly 35 Spanish ships reached home; most of the rest were wrecked on the Irish coast, whose people dealt harshly with survivors.

events.title: Prabhat Film Company Founded
events.blurb: Five filmmakers and one jeweller-financier pooled ₹15,000 in a Kolhapur courtyard and established a studio whose name meant "Dawn" — it would go on to produce landmark Marathi and Hindi films through the 1930s, win the first Venice Film Festival prize awarded to an Asian film, and whose abandoned compound would later house the country's national film school.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1929 — founded by V. Shantaram and associates. Their 1936 film Sant Tukaram won a Venice award. When the studio folded in 1953, its Pune premises became the site of the Film and Television Institute of India.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Awaara Released
events.blurb: A Raj Kapoor crime drama about a judge's illegitimate son — playing on the 1940s debate over heredity versus environment — became India's highest-grossing domestic release of the year and then, when dubbed and released abroad three years later, drew 64 million viewers in the Soviet Union alone, a record for any foreign film in that market. Its theme song became a street-singing anthem across Eurasia.
events.revealBlurb: December 14, 1951 — Raj Kapoor directed and starred. The song "Awaara Hoon" was so popular in the USSR, Turkey, and China that Soviet children grew up singing it phonetically in Hindi. Kapoor was reportedly stopped in Moscow streets for autographs.

events.title: Guide Released
events.blurb: A tourist guide who becomes first the manager and then the lover of a classical dancer, before his imprisonment transforms him into a reluctant holy man, gave Dev Anand his most demanding role and Waheeda Rehman her finest screen hour. Shot simultaneously in Hindi and English for two different markets, only the Hindi version became a classic; the English cut disappeared quietly.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 1965 (India) — directed by Vijay Anand, based on R.K. Narayan's 1960 Sahitya Akademi Award-winning novel The Guide. Narayan disliked the film adaptation. The English version, co-produced with a US studio, was screened briefly in America then shelved; a print was discovered decades later.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: The Fellowship of the Ring Released
events.blurb: A New Zealand director released the first of three films shot simultaneously in his homeland adapting a mid-20th-century English fantasy novel. The ensemble cast and landscape cinematography, the 5,000 days of digital effects by a Wellington-based studio, and the willingness to treat the fantasy material completely seriously pulled the genre from ghetto to respectability. The trilogy's final instalment would win 11 Oscars.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 2001 — Peter Jackson. The three films were shot over 438 days in New Zealand. Jackson's Weta Workshop became a world-leading effects house. The author's son Christopher Tolkien openly disliked the adaptations but inherited the royalty checks regardless.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Pullman Strike and Federal Injunction
events.blurb: When the Pullman Company cut wages by 25 percent without reducing rents in its company-owned town south of Chicago, nearly 4,000 workers walked out that spring; within weeks, the American Railway Union's boycott of Pullman cars had paralyzed rail traffic across 29 railroads and 27 states. President Grover Cleveland dispatched federal troops and obtained a court injunction to break the strike, establishing the federal government's willingness to use military force against organized labor.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1894 — Pullman, Illinois. Eugene Debs, the ARU leader, served six months in federal prison for defying the injunction — and read socialist literature in his cell, emerging as America's most famous socialist. The strike also created Labor Day as a federal holiday, rushed through Congress as a conciliation gesture two days before Debs was arrested.

events.title: 18th Amendment: Prohibition Ratified
events.blurb: Nebraska became the 36th state to ratify the 18th Amendment, providing the three-fourths supermajority needed to ban the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors in the United States. The amendment went into effect one year later, launching a 13-year experiment in moral legislation that spawned organized crime, enriched bootleggers, and ended with the 21st Amendment's repeal.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 1919 — ratified in less than 11 months, the fastest major amendment in history to that point. Al Capone made an estimated $60 million a year ($1.1 billion today) during Prohibition.

events.title: House Impeaches President Clinton
events.blurb: The House of Representatives voted to impeach President Bill Clinton on the 19th of that month, on charges of perjury before a grand jury (228–206) and obstruction of justice (221–212) arising from his false testimony about a sexual relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton became only the second U.S. president ever to be impeached; the Senate acquitted him on both articles the following February.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1998 — U.S. Capitol. The vote occurred while U.S. warplanes were bombing Iraq (Operation Desert Fox), which the White House denied was timed to distract from the impeachment. House Speaker-designate Bob Livingston resigned that same day. Clinton's approval rating on the day of his impeachment was 73%.

events.title: Hands Across America
events.blurb: Around 6.5 million Americans paid $10 each to stand along a 6,754-kilometre line stretching from a California beach to a New York skyscraper, holding hands for fifteen minutes as part of a charity event to raise money for hunger and homelessness relief. The line required one person every 0.77 metres; roughly half the route was inhabited uninterrupted, the rest had gaps. The event raised $34 million after expenses and was widely considered more spectacle than effective philanthropy.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1986 — organized by USA for Africa. The line ran from the Santa Monica Pier to the Battery in Manhattan via 16 states and DC. A theme song was recorded by over 500 celebrities. The event inspired the 2019 horror film "Us," where the hand-holding line takes on sinister significance.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network. The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.

events.title: A Trip to the Moon Released
events.blurb: A former stage magician released a 14-minute narrative film depicting a group of astronomers launched to the Moon in a giant bullet fired from a cannon, encountering hostile selenites, and returning to Earth. Its hand-tinted prints included the most recognizable image in early cinema: a cartoon Moon with a bullet lodged in its eye. It was pirated within months by Thomas Edison's company, which sold copies without paying royalties.
events.revealBlurb: 1902 — Georges Méliès, whose production company Star Film went bankrupt partly from lost piracy revenue. He destroyed many of his own negatives in bitterness; the hand-coloured version was rediscovered in Barcelona in 1993, disintegrating, and painstakingly restored.

events.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
events.blurb: Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature premiered at a Los Angeles theatre — a project industry insiders had dismissed throughout its three-year production as "Disney's folly" that would bankrupt the studio. 800 artists had drawn 250,000 individual cel frames. The 83-minute film made nearly $8 million in its first release on a budget of $1.5 million, rescued the studio's finances, and launched the modern feature-animation industry.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1937 — Carthay Circle Theatre, Los Angeles. Disney received an honorary Oscar consisting of one regular-sized statuette and seven miniature ones, presented by Shirley Temple. Adjusted for inflation, the film is still among the top-grossing of all time.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Avatar Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director returning to live-action feature filmmaking after a 12-year absence released a 162-minute science-fiction epic set on a moon orbiting a distant gas giant, shot with a new custom-built 3D camera system and populated by performance-captured 3-metre-tall blue aliens. The film's production had taken four years after the technology he needed had taken another decade. It became the highest-grossing film of all time and held the title for ten years.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2009 — James Cameron. The film grossed $2.9 billion on its initial run, briefly lost the title to Avengers: Endgame, then retook it with a 2021 re-release in China. Cameron had first written the treatment in 1994.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Oxygen Named and Combustion Explained
events.blurb: A French chemist named a newly isolated gas "oxygen" and demonstrated through careful weight measurements that combustion was not the release of a mysterious substance called phlogiston, but rather the combination of a material with this gas from the air. By showing that reactions in sealed systems conserved total mass, the work established quantitative chemistry as a discipline.
events.revealBlurb: 1778–1779 — Antoine Lavoisier's wife Marie-Anne translated English chemistry papers for him, drew the laboratory illustrations in his textbook, and helped design experiments. She is now recognised as an essential scientific collaborator, though her contributions went unacknowledged for two centuries. Lavoisier was guillotined in 1794; a judge reportedly said "the Republic has no need of scientists."

events.title: Radium Announced
events.blurb: A husband-and-wife chemistry team announced the isolation of a new radioactive element extracted from several tonnes of pitchblende ore, reporting it was approximately 900 times more radioactive than uranium. The woman researcher would go on to become the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different scientific disciplines.

events.title: Radium Discovered
events.blurb: After months of processing tonnes of uranium ore residue in a leaky shed, two researchers announced the existence of a second highly radioactive element — far more active per gram than uranium alone. The new element glowed faintly in the dark, making the laboratory notebooks radioactive enough to be hazardous even today. The work established radioactivity as an atomic property rather than a chemical reaction.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 1898 — Marie and Pierre Curie's notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protection; researchers must sign a waiver to view them in the French national library. Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).

events.title: Dolly the Sheep — First Cloned Mammal Announced
events.blurb: Scientists at a Scottish research institute announced the birth of a sheep cloned from a cell taken from an adult mammal's mammary gland — the first time a complex animal had been produced from a fully differentiated adult cell rather than an embryo. The achievement overturned a long-held belief that the DNA in adult cells had irreversibly lost its potential to generate a whole organism.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1997 — Dolly was born months earlier but kept secret while the team gathered data and published. She was named after the country singer Dolly Parton, because the cell donor was a mammary gland cell. Dolly developed arthritis and a lung disease unusually early, raising questions about whether cloned animals age faster — still debated today.

events.title: Emancipation Proclamation Takes Effect
events.blurb: President Abraham Lincoln's executive order declaring freedom for all enslaved people in Confederate states in active rebellion took legal effect at the new year, transforming the character of the war from a constitutional dispute over secession into an explicit struggle over slavery. The proclamation did not free enslaved people in border states still in the Union, but it authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army — eventually nearly 200,000 would serve.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1863 — Washington, D.C. Lincoln spent the morning shaking hundreds of hands at a White House reception; by the time he sat down to sign the Proclamation his hand trembled so badly he paused. "If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act," he said.

events.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Ratified in the aftermath of civil war, a constitutional amendment granted citizenship to "all persons born or naturalized in the United States," promised them equal protection under the laws, and guaranteed due process. Its sweeping language became, a century later, the foundation of Supreme Court rulings on school segregation, interracial marriage, abortion, and marriage equality.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1868 — citizenship via birthright. Its authors were thinking of formerly enslaved people; its practical effect reshaped virtually every area of American law. The "equal protection clause" alone has been cited in over 400 Supreme Court cases.

events.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott Ends
events.blurb: After 381 days of Black residents walking, carpooling, and riding Black-owned taxis rather than boarding segregated city buses, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower-court ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The next morning, Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks boarded an integrated bus in the front seats. The boycott had nearly bankrupted the transit system.
events.revealBlurb: December 20, 1956 — Martin Luther King rose to national prominence via the boycott. The organizing bureau ran car-pool lots that transported 30,000 people a day. Many Black women walked miles to work for over a year. "My feet is tired," one said famously, "but my soul is rested."

events.title: Watts Riots
events.blurb: A traffic stop of a Black motorist on a hot summer evening in a predominantly Black neighborhood of a California metropolis escalated into six days of unrest after police were accused of beating a pregnant bystander. 34 people died, 3,438 were arrested, and $40 million in property was destroyed over 120 square kilometres. The riots refocused national attention on Northern urban poverty, which the civil rights movement had largely ignored.
events.revealBlurb: August 11-16, 1965 — Watts, Los Angeles. A subsequent commission blamed police brutality and economic despair. Federal investment under the "Great Society" programs followed. Similar riots hit Detroit and Newark in 1967.

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: The Birth of a Nation Premieres
events.blurb: An American director released a three-hour silent film about a Southern family during the Civil War and Reconstruction, pioneering cinematic techniques that remain standard: close-ups, cross-cutting, battle-scene camera movement. The film portrayed the Ku Klux Klan as heroic and Black people (played mostly by white actors in blackface) as subhuman. Its release coincided with a revival of the real Klan, which had been inactive for 40 years.
events.revealBlurb: February 8, 1915 — D.W. Griffith at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles. President Woodrow Wilson hosted a White House screening, calling it "history written with lightning." The NAACP's protest against it was the organization's first major campaign.

events.title: Battleship Potemkin Released
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet director released a 75-minute silent film dramatizing a 1905 mutiny on a Russian imperial battleship. Its centerpiece, a massacre sequence on a flight of stone stairs in the Black Sea port city of Odessa, introduced a style of rapid associative editing that reshaped 20th-century cinema. A baby's pram bounces downward through the gunfire in a shot that has been quoted by dozens of later filmmakers.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1925 — Sergei Eisenstein. The Odessa Steps massacre is fictional; no such event occurred in 1905. The pram shot has been homaged in The Untouchables, Brazil, and The Simpsons. Joseph Goebbels reportedly called the film "a marvelous film without equal."

events.title: Gone with the Wind Premieres
events.blurb: A Hollywood producer premiered a 221-minute Civil War epic at a Southern U.S. theatre, 18 months of casting speculation and three and a half hours of runtime in the making. Parade crowds lined the streets; the event was broadcast on national radio. The film swept the Oscars and set a box-office record that, inflation-adjusted, has never been surpassed. Its racial politics — a romanticized view of the antebellum South and of slavery — have made its legacy contested.
events.revealBlurb: December 15, 1939 — Loew's Grand Theatre, Atlanta. Hattie McDaniel won Best Supporting Actress for her role as Mammy, the first African-American to win an Oscar. She was segregated to a side table at the ceremony and barred from the premiere itself.

events.title: Star Wars Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old American director released a science-fiction film mashing up elements of samurai cinema, WWII dogfight pictures, and Joseph Campbell's monomyth theory, with groundbreaking effects assembled in a repurposed warehouse with a workforce assembled from scratch. The studio had cut his budget and expected the film to flop; one executive had retitled it "The Adventures of Luke Starkiller." Lines began forming at theatres on opening morning and did not stop for years.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1977 — George Lucas. He traded his directing salary for merchandising rights; he became a billionaire. The effects company he had to build from scratch, Industrial Light & Magic, became the industry standard for decades. Campbell wept watching the film.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Battle of Bannockburn
events.blurb: A smaller Scottish army, dug in with wooden stakes around marshy ground near a castle in central Scotland, destroyed an invading English force three times its size over two days. The English king fled the field. The victory essentially secured Scottish independence, which would be formally recognized 14 years later at the Treaty of Northampton.
events.revealBlurb: June 23-24, 1314 — Robert the Bruce defeats Edward II. The Bruce allegedly split an English knight's skull with an axe in single combat before the main battle. Scotland's national flag flew over Stirling Castle the next morning.

events.title: Hundred Years' War Begins
events.blurb: An English king, claiming the French throne through his mother on the extinction of the main French royal line, formally renounced his homage for his continental territories and declared himself the rightful king of France. The resulting dynastic war would last 116 years across five generations, introduce the longbow as a battlefield weapon, and eventually produce the nation-states of France and England.
