events.revealBlurb: 1337 — Edward III vs. Philip VI. The conflict ran in spasms with long truces, and is named "Hundred Years" only in retrospect. Joan of Arc arrived in its fifth generation; gunpowder arrived in its fourth.

events.title: Chauvet Cave Paintings
events.blurb: Deep inside a limestone gorge in southern France, artists of the Upper Paleolithic ventured hundreds of metres into darkness with torches of burning pine and painted more than 400 animals onto the walls — rhinos, horses, cave lions, mammoths — using charcoal and red ochre. The images show sophisticated techniques: perspective, shading, motion. They would remain sealed behind a rockslide until rediscovered by three cavers in 1994.
events.revealBlurb: c. 30,000 BCE — Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc, Ardèche. Radiocarbon dating of the charcoal remains controversial; estimates span 32,000-30,000 BCE. A meticulous replica opened to tourists in 2015; the original site is restricted to scientists to preserve a fragile microclimate.

events.title: Parthenon Marbles Completed
events.blurb: Under the direction of a single master sculptor, a team of Athenian craftsmen completed the exterior sculptural programme of a temple on a fortified limestone hill above their city — a continuous carved frieze 160 metres long depicting a civic religious procession, plus 92 metopes and two pediments. The sculptures were painted in vivid colours; the bleached white appearance known to modern viewers is an accident of weathering.
events.revealBlurb: c. 438 BCE — Phidias, chief sculptor of the Parthenon in Athens. Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving marbles between 1801 and 1812 and sold them to the British Museum. Greece has been asking for them back for over 200 years.

events.title: The Last Supper Completed
events.blurb: An Italian polymath completed a 9-metre-wide mural in the refectory of a Dominican convent in a northern Italian city, depicting Christ announcing his betrayal and the instant of shocked reaction on the faces of his twelve disciples. The artist had worked on it for three years, painting in oil on a dry wall rather than true fresco — a choice that made the picture deteriorate visibly within his own lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: 1498 — Leonardo da Vinci in Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. His experimental technique began flaking within 20 years. The painting has been restored many times, most recently between 1978 and 1999. Allied bombing in 1943 destroyed the refectory roof but the wall survived.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: Van Gogh Cuts Off His Ear
events.blurb: After a violent argument with a fellow painter who had been living with him at a small yellow house in Provence for nine weeks, a 35-year-old Dutch artist cut off part of his own left ear with a razor, wrapped it in newspaper, and walked through the rain to deliver the package to a woman at a nearby brothel. He spent the night lying in a pool of blood. The fellow painter left the next morning. The injured man was committed to an asylum.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1888 — Vincent van Gogh; the houseguest was Paul Gauguin. He painted "Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear" within weeks. He sold only one painting in his lifetime and shot himself 19 months later in a Paris suburb.

events.title: First Human in Orbit
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet Air Force pilot rode a modified intercontinental ballistic missile into a single orbit reaching 327 km altitude, completing one lap of Earth in 108 minutes before ejecting from his capsule at 7 km and parachuting separately to a field in southern Russia. The mission was fully automated; Gagarin held an emergency manual-control key sealed in an envelope in case he needed it.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1961 — Vostok 1. Gagarin was chosen partly because he was 1.57 m tall and fit the cramped capsule. He shouted "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!") at liftoff — the same casual phrase Russian pilots use to start any flight. The module didn't fully separate and sent him spinning at 8 Gs before a wire bundle burned through.

events.title: First Mars Close-Up Flyby
events.blurb: Mariner 4 flew within 9,846 km of Mars and transmitted 21 photographs covering about 1% of the planet's surface — the first close-range images of another planet. The images revealed a cratered, Moon-like landscape and showed Mars had a much thinner atmosphere than expected, with a surface pressure of roughly 4–7 millibars, dashing hopes of a habitable world.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1965 — Mariner 4. The images took four days to receive and were so eagerly anticipated that JPL technicians printed the first strips of data by hand onto paper using artist's pastels, coloring by number before the computer could process the file. The result was a blurry colored rectangle they pinned to a bulletin board.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: Cassini Enters Saturn Orbit
events.blurb: The Cassini–Huygens spacecraft fired its main engine for 96 minutes to decelerate into Saturn orbit, threading a gap between the planet's F and G rings — a maneuver so precisely executed that the trajectory team reported it arrived within one kilometer of the planned position. Cassini became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, beginning a 13-year study of the planet and its moons.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 2004 — Cassini. Six months later, Cassini released the Huygens probe, which descended through Titan's atmosphere and transmitted data from its surface — the most distant landing ever achieved at the time. Cassini ultimately discovered that Enceladus has active geysers of water vapor, making it one of the top candidates for extraterrestrial life.

events.title: James Webb Space Telescope Launch
events.blurb: An Ariane 5 rocket launched the James Webb Space Telescope from Kourou, French Guiana, sending the largest and most complex space observatory ever built toward the second Lagrange point 1.5 million km from Earth. The 6.5-meter gold-coated beryllium mirror — too large to fit in the rocket fairing — had to fold origami-style and then unfurl over two weeks after launch.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 2021 — JWST. The telescope took 30 years and approximately $10 billion to build, surviving 17 major redesigns and two near-cancellations by Congress. Because the rocket had such a precise trajectory, JWST arrived at L2 with enough fuel margin to operate for 20 years instead of the planned 10. Its first image release on July 12, 2022 showed 13.1-billion-year-old light.

events.title: Marshall Plan Announced
events.blurb: At a Harvard commencement address, a U.S. Secretary of State proposed a massive economic recovery program for a continent devastated by six years of total war. Over four years, $13 billion in aid flowed to 16 western European nations, rebuilding factories, ports, and farms and tying their economies tightly to Washington.
events.revealBlurb: June 5, 1947 — George Marshall took ten minutes. The USSR and its satellites were invited to join; Stalin refused and forbade Poland and Czechoslovakia from participating. Adjusted for inflation, the plan would cost over $150 billion today.

events.title: Prague Spring Invasion
events.blurb: Reform-minded leaders in a central European capital had spent eight months experimenting with "socialism with a human face" — easing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and tolerating debate. In the night, 250,000 Warsaw Pact soldiers and 2,000 tanks rolled across the borders. Unarmed civilians tried to argue with the invading soldiers; within days the reforms were reversed.
events.revealBlurb: August 20-21, 1968 — invasion of Czechoslovakia. Reformist leader Alexander Dubček was flown to Moscow and forced to sign a capitulation. A student named Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square five months later in protest.

events.title: "Evil Empire" Speech
events.blurb: Addressing the National Association of Evangelicals in Florida, a U.S. president abandoned the detente rhetoric of his predecessors and described the rival superpower as "the focus of evil in the modern world." Speechwriters had lifted the phrase from a Star Wars reference. The framing shocked diplomats but reflected a deeper strategy: rhetorically delegitimize the opponent rather than coexist with it.
events.revealBlurb: March 8, 1983 — Ronald Reagan in Orlando. Speechwriter Tony Dolan had sneaked "evil empire" past the State Department, which had deleted it from earlier drafts. Two weeks later Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative.

events.title: Romanian Revolution
events.blurb: Within ten days, a dictator who had ruled a Balkan nation for 24 years lost control of a mass demonstration, fled the capital by helicopter, was captured, given a two-hour military tribunal, and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day alongside his wife. It was the only violent collapse among the eastern bloc regimes that fell at the time.
events.revealBlurb: December 16-25, 1989 — Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu. Soldiers actually had to be ordered to stop shooting them — they kept firing at the already-dead bodies. Ceaușescu's final request was to sing the Internationale. It was denied.

events.title: Soviet Union Dissolves
events.blurb: In a televised resignation speech, the last leader of a superpower announced the end of his office and, by implication, the end of the 69-year-old multinational state he had led for six and a half years. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered above the Kremlin for the final time and replaced with the Russian tricolor. Fifteen newly independent countries inherited the ruins.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1991 — Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation. The USSR formally ceased to exist the next day. Gorbachev lived another 31 years, mostly ignored at home and celebrated abroad, occasionally appearing in Pizza Hut and Louis Vuitton ads.

events.title: Great Chicago Fire
events.blurb: A fire started in a barn on a windy autumn evening in the second-largest U.S. metropolis and burned for 27 hours, destroying 17,500 buildings across 8.5 square kilometres of the central business district and killing around 300 people. A third of the city's population was left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: October 8-10, 1871 — Chicago. The Mrs. O'Leary's cow story is almost certainly a fabrication invented by a reporter who later confessed. On the very same day, the deadlier Peshtigo fire in Wisconsin killed 1,500+ people but is largely forgotten.

events.title: Galveston Hurricane
events.blurb: A Category 4 storm made landfall at a Gulf Coast barrier-island city, then the wealthiest in Texas, with a 4.6-metre storm surge that overtopped the highest point of the island. Roughly 8,000 people — nearly a quarter of the population — were killed in a single night. It remains the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1900 — Galveston, Texas. After the storm, the city built a 5-metre seawall and physically raised the entire island by up to 5 metres using sand pumped from the harbor. Houston, inland and safer, permanently overtook Galveston as the state's economic center.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon Spill
events.blurb: A blowout on a semi-submersible drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers and severed the riser pipe to a well 1,500 metres below the surface. Over the next 87 days, as engineers tried increasingly improbable methods to cap it, roughly 780 million litres of crude oil gushed into the sea — the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 2010 — off Louisiana. The well was finally killed in mid-September. BP paid over $65 billion in settlements, fines, and cleanup. A live-stream of the ocean-floor plume was watched by millions during the crisis; executives who claimed it was "relatively tiny" became memes.

events.title: Black Summer Bushfires
events.blurb: A prolonged drought and record heat fueled a six-month season of bushfires that burned 24 million hectares of southeastern Australia — an area larger than England. 33 people died directly; several hundred more from smoke. An estimated one billion wild animals perished. Smoke drifted across the Pacific and circled the globe.
events.revealBlurb: September 2019 – March 2020 — Australia. Images of koalas drinking from cyclists' water bottles and a town sheltering under blood-red skies went viral. Firefighters came from 12 countries. The season ended just as COVID-19 lockdowns began, compounding public trauma.

events.title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.blurb: Sepoys of the East India Company's Bengal Army, enraged by rumours that their rifle cartridges had been greased with beef and pork fat, rose in mutiny at a garrison town north of Delhi, shot their British officers, and marched south to proclaim a reluctant Mughal emperor the leader of a broader uprising. The revolt spread across north and central India over the following year.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1857 — Meerut. Bahadur Shah Zafar, the 82-year-old titular Mughal, was dragged out of retirement as figurehead. The revolt's brutal suppression ended Company rule in 1858; the British Crown took direct control of India.

events.title: Indian National Congress Founded
events.blurb: Seventy-two delegates — mostly English-educated Indian lawyers, journalists, and teachers, along with a few sympathetic Britons — met at a college in a western Indian port city for a three-day conference to petition the colonial government for greater Indian representation in its administration. The polite gathering would, over six decades, become the vehicle of a mass independence movement.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1885 — Bombay (now Mumbai). The prime mover was a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume, who believed organized political expression would prevent revolution. He was half right.

events.title: All-India Muslim League Founded
events.blurb: A group of aristocratic Muslim landowners, concerned that the Congress party would inadequately represent their community's political interests under any future system of representative government, formed a separate political organization at the close of an educational conference in a Bengali capital. It would eventually demand a separate Muslim-majority homeland, becoming the political vehicle of Pakistan.
events.revealBlurb: December 30, 1906 — Dhaka. Its initial demands were modest — reserved seats and weighted votes. Mohammad Ali Jinnah, who would lead it to the demand for Pakistan, did not even join until 1913, and left it in 1920 before returning.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Constitution of India Adopted
events.blurb: A constituent assembly of 299 members, chaired by a Bombay-trained lawyer from a once-"untouchable" community, completed two years and eleven months of debate to enact the longest written national constitution in the world — 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules — establishing a secular, socialist, democratic republic. It came into force on the anniversary of a 1930 declaration of complete independence.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 1950 — B.R. Ambedkar, chair of the drafting committee. The date — Republic Day — was chosen because it marked the 20th anniversary of Congress's Purna Swaraj declaration. The final handwritten copy is illuminated by the artist Nandalal Bose.

events.title: Amazon Founded
events.blurb: A former hedge-fund vice-president who had driven across the country from New York to Seattle with his wife, writing a business plan on the way, incorporated an online book retailer in the garage of a rented house in a Seattle suburb. He had chosen books because no single physical store could stock every book in print, but one big warehouse could. The company's first website was clunky; the logic was unstoppable.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1994 — Jeff Bezos. The company was originally called Cadabra; Bezos changed it after a lawyer misheard it as "cadaver." He considered and rejected relentless.com (now redirecting to Amazon).

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: Y2K Rollover
events.blurb: As the world's time zones successively crossed the boundary between the 20th and 21st centuries, decades of doomsday predictions — that computer systems storing years as two digits would interpret "00" as 1900 and crash vital infrastructure — largely failed to materialize. An estimated $300 billion had been spent worldwide on remediation code. Whether the peaceful transition vindicated the expense or exposed it as overblown remains contested.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 2000 — New Zealand and Pacific islands hit midnight first, without incident. Actual bugs did occur — a French meteorological satellite briefly misreported dates, some slot machines froze, a few nuclear plants had cooling-monitor glitches — but nothing catastrophic. The fix, written in COBOL in the 1990s, may be the largest software project ever.

events.title: Gangnam Style Hits 1 Billion Views
events.blurb: A music video by a 34-year-old South Korean rapper satirizing the upper-class culture of a Seoul neighborhood crossed a threshold no online video had previously reached, having accumulated a billion views on a major video platform in just over five months. Its horse-riding dance became a global meme and introduced a generation of Western audiences to K-pop. It broke the video platform's 32-bit view counter, forcing an engineering upgrade.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2012 — PSY's "Gangnam Style." It held the title of most-viewed YouTube video for five years before being overtaken by "Despacito." The counter overflow bug was quietly patched in 2014 when the video hit over 2 billion views.

events.title: Pokémon Go Released
events.blurb: A free mobile game combining augmented reality with a beloved monster-catching franchise launched initially in Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Within a week, 21 million daily active users were wandering streets and parks staring at their phones, discovering virtual creatures superimposed on physical landmarks. It became the fastest mobile game to reach $500 million in revenue and, more strikingly, got millions of sedentary users to walk outside.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Niantic Inc. Within weeks, fatal accidents, trespassing incidents, and a small bump in physical activity had all been documented. The Pokémon Go wedding, held in New York's Central Park, was among the odder cultural moments of mid-2016.

events.title: Parthenon Completed
events.blurb: A marble temple dedicated to the patron goddess of an Athenian acropolis was completed after fifteen years of work. The structure refined classical Doric proportions, incorporated subtle optical corrections (all its columns lean slightly inward, curved "entasis" swelling their shafts) so the temple appears perfectly rectilinear from a distance, and housed a 12-metre ivory-and-gold statue of Athena. It stood substantially intact for over 2,000 years until a Venetian shell hit a Turkish powder magazine inside it in 1687.
events.revealBlurb: 438 BCE — Ictinus and Callicrates, architects, under Phidias as sculptor. Built on the acropolis of Athens under Pericles. The Elgin Marbles, sold to the British Museum in 1816, are fragments of the Parthenon's sculptural programme — still the subject of Greek repatriation demands.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Panama Canal Opens
events.blurb: A 77-kilometre canal cutting across the narrowest part of the Central American isthmus opened to international shipping, after a US-run construction effort that had finished a French attempt abandoned two decades earlier amid malaria, yellow fever, and bankruptcy. The canal used a system of locks to raise ships 26 metres above sea level across the continental divide. It cut the sea route from New York to San Francisco by over 12,000 kilometres.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1914 — the ship SS Ancon made the first full transit. The American construction was made possible partly by controlling yellow fever and malaria through mosquito eradication. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties returned the canal to Panamanian sovereignty in 1999.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Burj Khalifa Opens
events.blurb: A 828-metre tapering skyscraper — Y-shaped in plan, with a buttressed central core — opened in a Gulf financial center as the tallest building in the world, dramatically taller than the previous record holder. Its construction had begun at the height of a regional real-estate bubble; by opening it had lost over 60 percent of its value and been taken over by a neighbouring emirate, after whose ruler the tower was hastily renamed. Its name had been "Burj Dubai" during construction.
events.revealBlurb: January 4, 2010 — architect Adrian Smith at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. The renamed "Burj Khalifa" honored Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, whose government bailed out Dubai during the financial crisis. Tom Cruise dangled from the outside in "Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol" (2011).

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Babe Ruth Sold to Yankees
events.blurb: A Boston baseball team's owner, needing cash to finance a Broadway musical he had invested in, sold the star pitcher and outfielder of his defending World Series champion team to the rival New York franchise for $100,000 cash plus a $300,000 loan secured by the team's stadium. The deal shipped the best player in baseball to the Yankees; Boston did not win another World Series for 86 years. Yankee championships followed in a cascade.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 1920 — Red Sox owner Harry Frazee sold Ruth to the Yankees. The musical was "No, No, Nanette" (1925); its eventual success does not redeem the sale. Ruth would hit 714 career home runs, lead the Yankees to 7 pennants, and define American sport for a generation.

events.title: Jesse Owens at Berlin Olympics
events.blurb: A 22-year-old African-American sprinter won four gold medals at a Summer Olympics held in the capital of a regime that had publicly declared the inferiority of his race. He took the 100m (10.3), 200m (20.7), long jump (8.06m), and 4×100m relay. His performance personally refuted Nazi racial theorizing on a stage the regime had built for its own glorification. He was welcomed home with a ticker-tape parade through New York but had to ride a freight elevator at his own Waldorf-Astoria reception because Black guests were not permitted in the main elevators.
events.revealBlurb: August 3-9, 1936 — Jesse Owens. The story that Hitler refused to shake his hand is disputed; Hitler had stopped shaking any medal winners' hands after the first day. President Roosevelt never congratulated Owens; Owens said later: "Hitler didn't snub me — it was our president who snubbed me."

events.title: Brady's Super Bowl LI Comeback
events.blurb: A New England Patriots team down 28-3 to the Atlanta Falcons in the third quarter of a Super Bowl came back to tie, forcing the first overtime in Super Bowl history, and won on a two-yard touchdown run that completed the largest comeback in title-game history. The team's 39-year-old quarterback won his record fifth Super Bowl championship and was named MVP for the fourth time. He would win two more Super Bowls over the following five years.
events.revealBlurb: February 5, 2017 — Super Bowl LI, Patriots 34, Falcons 28 OT, at NRG Stadium, Houston. Tom Brady. The Falcons had to stop themselves from ordering Super Bowl champion merchandise at halftime. Brady was the oldest Super Bowl MVP in history (at the time).

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: ENIAC Unveiled
events.blurb: Engineers at an American university publicly demonstrated an 27-tonne general-purpose electronic computer, filling a 30 by 15 metre room with 17,468 vacuum tubes, 10,000 capacitors, and 6,000 switches. The machine calculated artillery-shell trajectories 2,400 times faster than a human with an adding machine. Programming it required physically rewiring hundreds of cables; the programmers — all women — had to crawl inside to swap plugs.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1946 — University of Pennsylvania. Designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. Programmers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas, and Ruth Lichterman. They were not invited to the unveiling dinner; their faces were cropped out of celebratory photos for decades.

events.title: Altair 8800 Released
events.blurb: A cover article in an American hobbyist electronics magazine featured a $397 kit-build computer based on the Intel 8080 microprocessor, aimed at hardware enthusiasts willing to solder circuit boards and toggle binary instructions with front-panel switches. The magazine received over 2,000 kit orders in the first month. Among the Harvard students who saw the cover and wrote a BASIC interpreter for the machine were Bill Gates and Paul Allen.
events.revealBlurb: January 1975 — MITS Altair 8800, on the cover of Popular Electronics. Gates and Allen's BASIC would become the founding product of Microsoft. The Altair is universally credited as the first commercially successful microcomputer.

events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: IBM PC Released
events.blurb: The world's dominant mainframe computer maker released a small desktop machine built, unusually for the company, from off-the-shelf parts — an Intel 8088 processor, an operating system licensed from Microsoft, components any competitor could buy. Business customers trusted the name and bought millions. The design's open specifications led to a decade of "IBM compatible" clones that collectively made the Intel/Microsoft duopoly inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1981 — IBM PC model 5150. It had 16KB of RAM and no hard drive. IBM's decision to source DOS from Microsoft, rather than write it in-house, is usually cited as the great strategic error of 20th-century computing. Gates retained all distribution rights.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.
